name: Québec
note: Québec civil-law roles for incapacity, death and liquidation of successions under the Civil Code of Québec (CCQ) and Code of Civil Procedure (CCP), as amended by S.Q. 2020, c. 11 (in force 1 November 2022). Covers protection mandates, ordinary mandates, assistants, temporary representatives, tutors, consent to care, liquidators, organ donation, funeral arrangements and access to a deceased person's information. Consolidated texts were read from the official LégisQuébec PDFs marked 'Updated to April 7 2026'; later amendments, if any, were not checked. Federal roles are in ca-federal.

roles.name: Mandatary under a protection mandate (protection of the person)
roles.summary: A person of full age gives a protection mandate in anticipation of incapacity, by notarial act en minute or before 2 witnesses. It has no effect until incapacity is shown by medical and psychosocial assessment reports and the court, or a notary under the CCP, homologates it. The mandatary then consents to care and looks after the person's well-being. It ends when the court finds the mandator capable again, on revocation, or on either party's death.

roles.name: Assistant to a person of full age
localNames: assistant to a person of full age
roles.summary: Created by S.Q. 2020, c. 11, in force 1 November 2022. A person of full age who has a difficulty asks the Public Curator to recognize one or two assistants to help with decisions and act as intermediary with third parties. The person keeps full legal capacity, and the assistant cannot sign for them. Recognition is entered in a public register and lasts 3 years unless it ends sooner.

roles.name: Tutor to the person of full age
roles.summary: Since 1 November 2022 tutorship is Québec's only court protective regime for adults; curatorship and advisers were abolished. The court institutes tutorship when an adult cannot care for themself and needs representation. A tutor may be appointed to the person, to property, or both, and the court tailors the scope. The Public Curator acts only if appointed or if no tutor remains. Tutorship ends on a judgment of release or the adult's death.

localNames: personne qui démontre un intérêt particulier

roles.summary: When an adult is found incapable of consenting to care required by their state of health, and there are no advance medical directives, the mandatary or tutor consents. If there is none, consent comes from the married, civil union or de facto spouse. If there is no spouse or the spouse cannot act, it comes from a close relative or a person who shows a special interest. After death, the same person may consent to organ removal if the deceased's wishes are unknown.

roles.name: Liquidator of the succession designated by will
roles.summary: A testator may designate one or more liquidators. Anyone so designated, whether called executor or administrator, is a liquidator. From the opening of the succession at death, the liquidator exercises the seisin of the heirs with no court grant. A notarial will needs no probate, but a holograph or witnessed will must first be probated by the court or a notary. Liquidation ends with the final account and discharge.

notes.text: Inventory is mandatory (published in the register) unless all heirs and successors exempt the liquidator, which makes them liable beyond the property they take.
For use outside Québec, an interested person may get letters of verification certifying that the succession has opened and who the liquidator is.

If liquidation takes more than a year, the liquidator must render an annual account. If the succession is not manifestly solvent, debts and legacies may not be paid until 60 days after the notice of closure of inventory.

The court designates or replaces a liquidator when heirs disagree or no one can be appointed. There is no grant of administration.

roles.name: Person consenting to post-mortem organ or tissue removal
localNames: personne qui pouvait consentir aux soins
roles.summary: Québec uses opt-in consent. A person of full age, or a minor 14 or over, may give organs or tissues, verbally before 2 witnesses or in writing, including through the RAMQ register or the notaries' register. The wishes must be followed unless there is a compelling reason not to. If the deceased's wishes are unknown, the person who was or would have been qualified to consent to their care (usually the spouse or a close relative) may consent.

poaDurableByDefault.note: No yes/no answer fits. Art 2175 does not list the mandator's incapacity as terminating an ordinary mandate: the mandate 'may' end 'in certain cases' on tutorship or homologation of a protection mandate, and it continues during homologation proceedings (art 2167.1). But a mandate given in anticipation of incapacity (protection mandate) takes effect only on homologation (art 2166).

springingPoaAllowed.note: A protection mandate is by nature conditional on incapacity, but it springs only on court (or notary) homologation after medical and psychosocial assessments, not on a private confirmation.

poaRegistrationBeforeUse.note: No registry filing is required. Instead a protection mandate needs homologation (a judicial or notarial proceeding) before it can be performed. After the 2020 reform, the mandatary must make an inventory within 60 days and render periodic accounts.

healthAgentStartsOn.note: The protection mandatary acts only after homologation. Without a mandatary or tutor, the spouse or a close relative consents to care once incapacity is ascertained (art 15).

supportedDecisionMakingStatute.name: Assistant to a person of full age (arts 297.10 ff. CCQ), added by S.Q. 2020, c. 11, in force 1 November 2022
supportedDecisionMakingStatute.note: The assistant is recognized by the Public Curator and entered in a public register. The assisted person keeps full capacity, and recognition lasts 3 years.

digitalAssetsFiduciaryStatute.note: No Québec provision on fiduciary access to digital assets was found in the CCQ or related statutes reviewed. The ULCC uniform act is a common-law model and has not been enacted in Québec. Liquidators rely on seisin (art 777) and their general functions (arts 776, 802-804).

onlineToolsRecognisedInLaw.note: No Québec enactment recognizes platform online-tool designations.

organDonationModel.name: Civil Code of Québec arts 43-44; consent registers kept by RAMQ (L.Q. 2010, c. 38) and the Chambre des notaires
organDonationModel.note: Express consent, or consent from the person qualified to consent to care when wishes are unknown. Bill 194 (presumed consent) passed adoption in principle 104-0 on 9 June 2023 but was not assented; it is not law.

smallEstateWithoutGrant.note: Québec has no grant system. The liquidator (or the heirs by law) has seisin from death without court authority, and only holograph or witnessed wills need probate. The only statutory simplified route is liquidation by the heirs' agreement of a manifestly solvent succession (art 779), with no value threshold and at the cost of unlimited personal liability for debts. No statutory monetary threshold was found; bank release practices are not law.

probateGrantName.value: none (no grant); probate (vérification) of holograph and witnessed wills; letters of verification for use outside Québec
probateGrantName.note: There is no grant of probate or administration. A notarial will is an authentic act and needs no probate, so the liquidator acts from the opening of the succession. Holograph wills and wills made before witnesses must be probated by the Superior Court or a notary (CCQ art 772; CCP arts 312, 459-462). Letters of verification (CCP art 463) prove the liquidator's capacity outside Québec.

deceasedPersonalDataProtected.note: Québec's private-sector Act (P-39.1, amended by Law 25, S.Q. 2021, c. 25) and the health information Act (R-22.1, S.Q. 2023, c. 5) protect deceased persons' information and set specific access rights. Liquidators, heirs and beneficiaries get access only as it affects their rights. Spouses and close relatives may get information that helps grieving (P-39.1 s 40.1, in effect from the September 2023 Law 25 phase) unless the deceased refused in writing. Private-sector information may be communicated without consent 30 years after death.

healthAgentPostDeathAuthority.note: A protection mandate terminates on the mandator's death (art 2175). The mandatary must still do what cannot be deferred without risk of loss, notify the Public Curator and render account (arts 2182-2184). Funeral decisions go to heirs or successors (art 42), and organ consent to the person who was qualified to consent to care (art 44).
